routes.description: Religiously inherited narratives and value hierarchies embody evolved practical knowledge that makes coherent moral action and durable meaning possible.
routes.successCriteria: Show that action necessarily presupposes an ultimate value structure, that religious traditions substantially embody it, and that secular practice cannot simply detach from that inheritance.

motionBridge.description: Humans need a God-function or religiously inherited value structure to organize meaning, morality, suffering, and action.

centralBridges.description: Conduct reveals operative belief more reliably than explicit self-description does.
Stable secular institutions continue to enact inherited Judeo-Christian commitments.
Durable meaning must sustain people through tragedy rather than merely produce happiness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Long-standing religious patterns reflect biological-cultural selection rather than arbitrary cultural copying.

routes.description: Naturalistic, memetic, and contemplative processes can explain constructed meaning and ethical conduct without God or continuing religious commitment.
routes.successCriteria: Show that humans construct workable meanings and moral practices from evolved needs, culture, reflection, and social experience, while religious belief is neither necessary nor reliably beneficial.

motionBridge.description: Humans can make sense of life and act morally without God or an indispensable religious foundation.

centralBridges.description: Meaning emerges from biological needs, cultural evolution, and personal or social construction.
Compassion, gratitude, and moral conduct can develop through secular reflection and practice.
Religiosity does not reliably predict healthier or more functional societies.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Religion can persist as a culturally copied meme complex containing both beneficial and harmful features.

currentSections.title: Belief, action, and secular ethics
currentSections.rationale: This exchange establishes whether conduct requires religious belief and whether contemplative practice can independently ground ethical behavior.

currentSections.title: Religious stories and cultural evolution
currentSections.rationale: This section tests whether inherited stories embody indispensable archetypal knowledge or remain culturally transmitted and contestable constructions.

currentSections.title: Secular societies and inherited morality
currentSections.rationale: The speakers directly contest empirical social outcomes and whether modern moral institutions remain dependent on religious inheritance.

currentSections.title: Meaning, tragedy, and the God-function
currentSections.rationale: The final exchanges confront constructed meaning, nihilism, action, and the definition of God most directly at motion level.

moves.proposition: Operative belief is principally disclosed by action, because people lack transparent access to their own thoughts.
Meditative observation can produce compassionate and kind conduct without rational deduction or an underlying divine basis.
Compassion alone cannot ground a complex society because a short-term caregiving disposition does not supply a complete adult ethic.
Religions are mixed meme complexes whose persistence reflects beneficial features as well as harmful ones, though their net effect may remain negative.
Religious archetypes are biologically grounded patterns of behavior and representation rather than merely contagious ideas.
Biologically inherited archetypal tendencies and culturally copied memes are distinct, and archetypal material can subsequently become memetic.
Biblical stories were formulated as responses to tragedy and malevolence and function as inherited cultural antidotes to those conditions.
Removing the religious cornerstone risks nihilism and totalitarian replacement because inherited value structures cannot be recreated at will.
Observed correlations between stronger proclaimed religiosity and social dysfunction undermine the claim that losing God predictably worsens societies.
Secular stability persists because Western societies still enact Judeo-Christian commitments to individual sovereignty and honest speech.
Contemporary secular Britain and Scandinavian societies provide live examples of functioning welfare-oriented societies without majority religious commitment.
Humans seek meaning deep enough to sustain them through tragedy, which is categorically different from seeking happiness.
Accepting ultimate meaninglessness can coexist with ordinary purposive action because evolved creatures naturally continue responding to needs and interests.
Continued purposive action contradicts lived acceptance of meaninglessness because acting on priorities treats them as meaningful.
Higher meanings are constructed through memetic evolution in language and culture layered upon biological needs.
Whatever occupies the top of a person's necessary value hierarchy performs the function of God, regardless of professed belief or naming.
